interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: LLM Agents Factory: Retrieval of Domain-Specific LLM Agents
papers.authors: Vitalii Belov , Artyom Sosedka , Andrey Sakhovskiy , Elizaveta Kovtun , Artyom Boyarskikh , Semen Budennyy
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents improve task performance by decomposing problems into role-specialized behaviors. However, their practical deployment is often limited by the computational cost and instability associated with the on-the-fly agent design for each user request. To address this, we present LLM Agents Factory, a retrieval-based framework that constructs domain-specific and Wikipedia-grounded agents on demand using a base of over 20K predetermined agent profiles. Our framework supports two modes: (1) agent profile retrieval via semantic search and (2) distillation into a compact model fine-tuned for direct agent generation. Experiments on MMLU, BIG-bench, and BIG-bench Hard in a single-agent scenario demonstrate that our retrieval-based agent construction surpasses non-agent baselines in accuracy while matching AutoGen generation quality with a 120B backbone at a substantially lower inference cost. Our work reveals that retrieval from a structured agent repository provides a cost-efficient, accurate, and controllable alternative to dynamic agent generation, responding to the strict demands of industrial applications. We provide the implementation code and the agent base in this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: The paper proposes a retrieval-based framework for constructing domain-specific LLM agents, which could be adapted for astronomical research agents. It emphasizes cost-efficiency and controllability, relevant for building specialized agents for JWST data analysis.
papers.Short digest: The paper addresses the high computational cost and instability of designing LLM agents on-the-fly for each request. It introduces LLM Agents Factory, a retrieval-based system with over 20K pre-defined agent profiles, which can either retrieve an agent via semantic search or distill into a compact model for direct generation. This could matter for astronomy by enabling efficient, specialized agents for tasks like source classification or SED fitting without heavy compute. I could imagine using it to build a repository of agents for different JWST analysis workflows, such as one for photometric redshift estimation or another for spectral fitting. However, the paper tests on general NLP benchmarks (MMLU, BIG-bench), so I should check if the agent profiles are domain-agnostic or if they can be customized for astronomy-specific tasks.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the agent profiles are domain-specific or generic, and whether they can be customized for astronomy tasks.
Look for details on how the retrieval base is constructed and whether it includes scientific domains.
Examine the distillation process and whether it can be applied to smaller models for deployment on limited compute.

papers.title: Evaluating Semantic and Spatial Guidance for Foundation Model Segmentation of Small-Scale PV in Remote Sensing Imagery
papers.authors: Roni Blushtein-Livnon , Tal Svoray , Osher Rafaeli , Michael Dorman , Itay Fischhendler , Havazelet Yahel , Emir Galilee
papers.abstract: Spatio-temporal PV data are essential for understanding adoption processes in off-grid regions, yet such data remain largely unavailable. Automated segmentation of remote sensing (RS) imagery offers a promising solution; yet, residential PV systems remain challenging targets because of their small size and sparse distribution, resulting in severe target-background imbalance. Vision-language foundation models (FMs) provide a data-efficient paradigm through prompt-based semantic and spatial guidance, but the relative contribution of different prompt types remains unclear. We systematically evaluate SAM3 for small-scale PV segmentation in RS imagery by comparing textual, geometric, and hybrid prompting, under varying supervision levels, training strategies, spatial resolutions, and imaging conditions. Multi-temporal aerial imagery from a large off-grid rural region serves as a study site, with findings validated across three additional datasets. Prompting strategy emerged as the dominant factor governing model behavior. Textual prompting consistently produced the lowest performance and showed the greatest sensitivity to supervision and imaging conditions. In contrast, spatial guidance substantially improved both segmentation accuracy and robustness. Hybrid prompting achieved the highest accuracy and stability, indicating that semantic and spatial guidance provide complementary information. Most performance gains were achieved with only a few hundred annotated samples, demonstrating strong data efficiency. Transfer learning had limited overall impact, with only modest improvements observed for textual prompting under limited supervision. Overall, our findings establish prompting strategy as a key determinant of SAM3 adaptation, robustness, and generalization, highlighting the potential of promptable FMs for scalable PV mapping in data-constrained off-grid regions.
papers.Reasons for match: Evaluates vision-language foundation models for small object segmentation in remote sensing, directly relevant to astronomical source detection and classification. The prompting strategies and data efficiency insights could transfer to JWST or survey imagery.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks how different prompting strategies (textual, geometric, hybrid) affect segmentation of small-scale solar panels in remote sensing imagery using SAM3. It finds that spatial guidance (geometric prompts) substantially improves accuracy over textual prompts, and hybrid prompting is best. For astronomy, this suggests that using spatial priors (e.g., coordinates or masks) with foundation models could improve detection of small sources like high-redshift galaxies or little red dots. One could try this on JWST images with point-source or extended-source prompts. A caveat is that the study is on aerial imagery, so transfer to astronomical data needs validation.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the prompting strategies are applicable to astronomical images with different noise and background.
Look for details on how many annotated samples are needed for good performance, which is relevant for limited labeled data.
See if the model can handle multi-band or multi-wavelength inputs, as JWST data are often multi-filter.

papers.title: REATS: LLM Reasoning-based Ensemble Learning for Adaptive Time Series Forecasting
papers.authors: Xu Zhang , Chang Xu , Hui Sun , Nan Ma , Zijian Zhang , Peng Wang , Wei Wang , Li Zhao
papers.abstract: Due to the diversity of real-world time series, no single forecasting model consistently dominates across all samples. Ensemble learning addresses this by combining complementary model strengths, yet existing methods rely on fixed rules or black-box models based solely on numerical inputs, failing to leverage LLM reasoning for interpretable weighting decisions. We propose REATS, which leverages LLM reasoning capabilities as an intelligent ensemble router that jointly processes textual temporal pattern descriptions and numerical features to produce interpretable, sample-adaptive ensemble weights through chain-of-thought reasoning. To enable effective LLM-based ensembling, we study its key design choices and propose: (i) a structured input pipeline that transforms raw time series into hybrid textual--numerical representations with fixed token cost, enabling rule-based chain-of-thought construction without API dependency, augmented with retrieved similar-sample priors; (ii) a diverse multi-row weight supervision scheme coupled with a token-efficient percentage-table format that reduces numerical complexity and mitigates LLM hallucinations; and (iii) a two-stage fine-tuning framework combining SFT with GRPO, where a reciprocal reward mapping transforms the continuous unbounded MSE gap into bounded signals with amplified near-oracle sensitivity, addressing the uniform sensitivity and outlier-dominated advantage compression inherent in naive reward designs for regression-based GRPO. Experiments on eight benchmarks demonstrate that REATS outperforms competitive ensemble baselines while providing natural language explanations and demonstrating strong transfer learning and out-of-domain generalization to unseen candidate models.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper uses LLM reasoning for ensemble forecasting, which could transfer to time-series analysis in astronomy (e.g., light curves or photometric data). However, it is not directly astronomical and lacks multimodal or survey-specific focus.
papers.Short digest: The paper addresses the problem that no single time-series forecasting model works for all data, and proposes an LLM-based ensemble router that combines textual pattern descriptions with numerical features to produce interpretable, sample-adaptive weights. The main idea is to use chain-of-thought reasoning in an LLM to decide which forecasting model to trust for each sample, with a structured input pipeline and fine-tuning. For astronomy, this could help combine multiple models for light-curve or variability analysis, but the method is generic and not tested on astronomical data. A concrete workflow might be applying it to multi-wavelength light curves to improve classification or prediction. Before investing time, check if the method scales to long, irregularly sampled astronomical time series and whether the textual descriptions are feasible for large surveys.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method handles irregularly sampled or missing data, common in astronomical time series
Look for details on how textual pattern descriptions are generated and whether they can be automated for large datasets
Evaluate the transfer learning results to see if the method generalizes to unseen model types, which is relevant for diverse survey data

papers.title: EvoMem: Memory-Augmented Evolution for Code Optimization
papers.authors: Viktor Volkov , Valentin Khrulkov , Andrey V. Galichin , Danil Sivtsov , Nikita Glazkov , Olga Volkova , Konstantin Pchelin , Iaroslav Bespalov , Dmitry V. Dylov , Petr Anokhin , Ivan Oseledets
papers.subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE)
papers.abstract: Successful mutation strategies in evolutionary code search may contain reusable knowledge that is useful beyond a single run, and in some cases may transfer across related tasks and domains. However, existing LLM-driven evolutionary frameworks largely discard such knowledge, repeatedly rediscovering similar ideas and limiting opportunities for cross-run and cross-task learning. We introduce EvoMem, a persistent memory architecture for LLM-based evolutionary program search that captures and reuses candidate mutation knowledge. EvoMem converts successful mutation events into structured, task-aware advice for future runs. It operates in two phases: after each run, it extracts and stores promising ideas with provenance, and during subsequent evolution, it retrieves a small set of relevant instructions based on the current task and program context to guide mutation. Across geometric optimization, multi-hop question answering, GPU kernel optimization, and related benchmarks, our experiments show positive average improvements in target metrics or search speed for most evaluated settings, while also revealing variability across tasks. Overall, EvoMem provides evidence that persistent memory can reduce some redundant exploration and improve the reuse and adaptation of successful strategies in LLM-driven evolutionary search.
papers.Reasons for match: Focuses on LLM-driven evolutionary code optimization with memory reuse, which could transfer to automated scientific workflows like optimizing data-reduction or fitting code. Not astronomy-specific but the idea of persistent memory for search could inspire research-agent designs.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks whether successful mutation strategies in LLM-based evolutionary program search can be reused across runs and tasks. It introduces EvoMem, a persistent memory that stores successful mutation ideas and retrieves them to guide future mutations. This could matter for astronomy by enabling automated tools that learn from past data-analysis or modeling attempts. One could imagine using it to optimize a photometric redshift or SED-fitting code across many datasets. A caveat is that gains vary by task, so it may not always improve performance.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether memory retrieval is based on task context or program structure, and how relevant it would be to astronomy code.
Look for benchmarks that resemble scientific or numerical optimization, not just geometric or QA tasks.
See if the method requires a large number of runs to build useful memory, which may be costly for astronomy workflows.

papers.title: MIRA: Medical Image Reflection for Agentic Diagnosis
papers.authors: Shengzhi Wang , Jun Yang , Kai Wu , Xiaozhong Ji , Yiwen Ye , Ziyang Chen , Mingliang Xiong , Wen Fang , Mingqing Liu , Mengyuan Xu , Miaoxuan Shan , Caiyan Liu , Bin He , Qingwen Liu
papers.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
papers.abstract: Medical visual agents can use tools to inspect images and retrieve external knowledge, but indiscriminate tool use may introduce noisy or misleading evidence. Reliable diagnosis therefore requires not only acquiring additional observations, but also verifying whether tool actions are necessary and whether the resulting evidence supports the current hypothesis. We introduce MIRA (Medical Image Reflection for Agentic Diagnosis), a medical visual diagnostic framework for autonomous evidence search and reflective verification. MIRA dynamically invokes image-processing operations, including zooming, grounding, pointing, rotation, and measurement, as well as web search, while evaluating the relevance and consistency of the acquired evidence. We develop MIRA through a two-stage training strategy. First, a tool-augmented Monte Carlo Tree Search data engine explores diverse diagnostic hypotheses and jointly verifies visual grounding accuracy and semantic consistency to construct supervised fine-tuning trajectories. Second, reinforcement learning further improves decision-making through online reflective principle evolution: failure cases are distilled into candidate principles, and only principles that improve held-out rollout rewards are retained. Across nine medical visual reasoning benchmarks, MIRA achieves an average score of 64.73, improving its Qwen3-VL-8B backbone by 7.44 points. It also increases useful tool-use judgments from 56.2% to 73.8% and reduces harmful judgments from 8.9% to 1.6%. Qualitative analyses show that MIRA can re-examine evidence, correct premature conclusions, and adapt its tool-use strategy. Project page: this https URL
papers.Reasons for match: Agentic diagnosis with reflective verification, directly relevant to research agents for scientific discovery. The tool-use and evidence verification framework could transfer to astronomical data analysis.
papers.Short digest: The paper introduces MIRA, a medical visual agent that uses tools like zooming and web search, with reflective verification to ensure evidence supports the diagnosis. It improves tool-use judgments and reduces harmful actions. For astronomy, this could inspire agents that inspect images, query catalogs, and verify hypotheses, e.g., for classifying little red dots. However, the method is trained on medical data and may need adaptation.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the reflection mechanism can be applied to non-medical domains.
Look for details on the tool set and whether it can be extended to astronomical tools.
See if the training pipeline requires large amounts of annotated data, which may be scarce in astronomy.
